question: Can correctness or toxicity transfer across datasets be predicted from the ordered layerwise changes of every token's residual-stream state, rather than from a static hidden state at one selected layer?

key_findings.claim: Truth as a Trajectory (TaT) is a supervised candidate ranker over a flattened token-by-layer grid of residual-stream displacements, not an unsupervised truth detector or an analysis of a model-generated reasoning chain.
key_findings.evidence: For each supplied continuation, the authors run the frozen model separately, compute d[t,l] = h[t,l+1] - h[t,l], concatenate all N x L updates in token-major order, and feed the sequence to an LSTM plus sigmoid head trained on correctness labels. At evaluation, the system selects among supplied candidates; it does not generate, verify, or localize intermediate reasoning steps.

key_findings.claim: Simple scalar kinematics are a reported negative result: even an oracle-guided search over velocity, acceleration, jerk, two curvature definitions, and arc length does not yield a consistent correctness rule.
key_findings.evidence: On Llama-3.1-8B, velocity is sometimes the strongest descriptor but no descriptor consistently matches normalized-log-likelihood accuracy across ARC-Easy, OpenBookQA, StoryCloze, and TruthfulQA. Qwen2.5-14B is less consistent, and continuation-only, last-token-only, and layer-mean trajectory variants degrade further. Because the descriptor rules are selected with ground-truth knowledge, these plots are an upper-bound diagnostic rather than a deployable baseline.

key_findings.claim: A source-trained TaT reader often transfers better than the exact-middle-layer linear probe, with the strongest Llama donors being ARC-Challenge, ARC-Easy, and OpenBookQA.
key_findings.evidence: Across nine Llama-3.1-8B reasoning targets, ARC-C-trained TaT has 79.63 average, 82.17 ID, and 79.31 OOD accuracy versus 71.03/75.32/70.49 for the probe; ARC-E gives 77.76/89.10/76.34 versus 72.44/83.99/71.00; OpenQA gives 78.38/90.80/76.83 versus 67.11/83.15/65.11. The weaker BoolQ and SocialIQA donors yield TaT averages of only 56.58 and 65.03, so donor choice remains consequential.

key_findings.claim: The prose overstates TaT's advantage over the frozen model's few-shot baseline and understates its losses to probing.
key_findings.evidence: The paper says TaT consistently surpasses zero- and few-shot base performance, but the eight TaT donor-row averages exceed the 75.7 few-shot average only for ARC-C, ARC-E, and OpenQA (3/8); they exceed the 67.9 zero-shot average for 6/8. Several probe losses are not marginal: OpenQA-trained TaT scores 56.50 on HellaSwag versus 70.26 for the probe, CosQA-trained TaT scores 64.05 on ComQA versus 77.34, and SocialIQA-trained TaT scores 55.69 on ComQA versus 72.16. Moreover, TaT uses labeled source-task training and scores every candidate, whereas the base baseline is not given comparable supervised adaptation.

key_findings.claim: Against rank-16 LoRA trained on ARC-Easy, TaT transfers better on five of six reported tasks, but not on BoolQ.
key_findings.evidence: TaT versus LoRA selection accuracy is 94.98 versus 83.76 on StoryCloze, 77.20 versus 52.40 on OpenQA, 89.10 versus 85.98 on ARC-Easy, 73.81 versus 61.26 on ARC-Challenge, and 79.19 versus 75.86 on HellaSwag. BoolQ reverses the result, 78.56 for TaT versus 79.97 for LoRA. This is the paper's closest adaptation comparison, but it uses one donor and does not match trainable parameters, scoring cost, or objective.

key_findings.claim: Displacement improves OOD toxicity detection in three of four model rows, not consistently in all four, and raw trajectories dominate most in-distribution toxicity cells.
key_findings.evidence: On ToxiGen, displacement/raw/probe accuracy is 84.23/81.99/79.62 for Llama-3.1-8B, 82.28/83.48/72.58 for Qwen2.5-14B, 82.34/81.93/75.16 for Qwen3-30B MoE, and 81.40/80.22/62.24 for Qwen3-32B. Thus the caption's 'consistently best' claim is contradicted by Qwen2.5-14B. On RealToxicityPrompts standard and challenging splits, raw trajectories win all eight model-split comparisons; for Qwen3-30B MoE challenging, displacement falls to 87.66 versus 98.92 raw and 94.50 probe.

key_findings.claim: The central displacement advantage is task-dependent: a raw-state LSTM is stronger for two of three reasoning donors, while displacement has a large advantage only for OpenBookQA.
key_findings.evidence: OOD accuracy for raw versus displacement trajectories is 83.62 versus 79.31 when trained on ARC-C and 76.55 versus 76.34 for ARC-E, but 69.85 versus 76.83 for OpenQA. The evidence supports displacement as a useful lexical/prompt-shift bottleneck in some settings, not as a uniformly necessary representation. No direct lexical counterfactual or wording-reconstruction audit establishes that the difference is caused by lexical-confound removal.

key_findings.claim: Both axes and their ordering can matter, although the final-token column is almost sufficient for ARC-Easy.
key_findings.evidence: For an ARC-C donor, full-grid TaT reaches 79.31 OOD versus 70.41 for one middle-layer row and 73.68 for the final-token column. For ARC-E, full grid is 76.34 versus 70.78 and 76.08, leaving only a 0.26-point gain over final-token-only. Replacing the LSTM with an order-invariant Set MLP reduces OOD from 79.31 to 73.17 (ARC-C), 76.34 to 72.75 (ARC-E), and 76.83 to 72.70 (OpenQA), even though Set MLP slightly wins ARC-E ID, 89.90 versus 89.10.

key_findings.claim: The Qwen2.5-14B appendix supports cross-task transfer over a smaller four-target grid, but it does not establish one architecture-invariant detector.
key_findings.evidence: For OpenQA, ARC-C, and ARC-E donors, TaT OOD averages are 82.65, 83.66, and 85.58 versus 65.97, 74.74, and 72.08 for model-specific probes. Each detector is nevertheless trained and evaluated inside one frozen model; there is no cross-model transfer of a single classifier. The paper also inconsistently names its larger models as Qwen2.5-30B/32B in the setup but Qwen3-30B MoE/Qwen3-32B in Table 3.

key_findings.claim: The measured classifier overhead is small in parameters and memory but material in latency; the claimed negligible embedded overhead is not measured.
key_findings.evidence: Against an fp16 Llama-3.1-8B forward pass with 8.0B parameters, 64.0 ms latency, and about 15,000 MB, the 4.76M-parameter LSTM adds 10.5 ms (reported as 16%) and 18.1 MB. The timing covers separate full-activation extraction and LSTM evaluation. The caption asserts that embedding the classifier within layers would be negligible, but supplies no pipelined benchmark and omits the cost of one frozen-model forward pass per candidate.

key_findings.claim: The appendices qualify both optimization and the probe baseline: TaT uses validation-selected hyperparameters and three-seed averages, while a single static probe depth has no universal optimum.
key_findings.evidence: The authors sweep learning-rate and regularization choices, LSTM hidden size 128-512, and one to three LSTM layers, run each training session with three seeds, average it, and select by source validation performance; most chosen models use width 128 and two or three layers. The linear probe takes the final continuation token at the exact middle layer. A -1 through -16 sweep peaks at -15 for ARC-C (0.7188), -13 for ARC-E (0.7384), and -15 for OpenQA (0.6924), confirming layer sensitivity but not comparing TaT to a validation-selected best-layer probe in the main grid.

anchors.section: Appendix C-D / Implementation and probe-layer sensitivity

method.core_idea: Treat transformer depth as an ordered dynamical trajectory and train a lightweight reader on residual updates rather than on an activation snapshot, with the aim of retaining how a representation changes while suppressing persistent token and prompt content.
method.mechanism: For every prompt-candidate pair, the frozen base model emits residual states for every token after every block. TaT differences adjacent layers, flattens the resulting N-token by L-layer grid into one M=NxL sequence, and passes it through an LSTM; the last recurrent state is classified by a sigmoid head. A labeled source dataset trains one model-specific reader, and target tasks are evaluated without target-specific reader updates. The main comparator is a linear classifier on the candidate's final-token state at the exact middle transformer layer; additional controls use raw states in the same LSTM, one grid row, one grid column, an order-invariant per-update MLP with mean pooling, rank-16 LoRA, and hand-crafted scalar kinematics.
assumptions: Every reasoning item supplies a finite candidate set with an unambiguous correct continuation, and candidate selection accuracy is an adequate proxy for reasoning validity.
A separate full forward pass and residual-stream trace are available for every candidate; the method cannot operate through a text-only model API.
Persistent lexical and token-identity components cancel sufficiently under adjacent-layer differencing, while correctness-relevant updates remain in a shared residual-stream basis.
Token-major flattening of a token-by-layer grid defines a meaningful sequential order that an LSTM can exploit.
A labeled source task contains a transferable correctness or toxicity signature rather than a source-specific shortcut, and source validation selects hyperparameters that remain useful OOD.
The exact-middle-layer probe is a representative static baseline even though the best layer varies by dataset.
Ranking candidates by separate binary scores does not require calibrated probabilities or a portable standalone threshold.
ToxiGen constitutes a lexical-confound stress test for a reader trained on RealToxicityPrompts, even though the experiment does not use matched lexical counterfactuals.
Results from separately trained readers across base-model families can support an architecture-level pattern even though no classifier transfers between models.

techniques.role: Transforms each state into the update written by the next transformer block, attenuating components persistent across adjacent layers.
Exposes every token and every depth as one ordered sequence rather than selecting a single layer or token.
Learns nonlinear, order-sensitive signatures over a variable-length sequence of residual updates.
Separates source-task fit from off-diagonal transfer by training on one benchmark and evaluating all others.
Tests whether the representational bottleneck, rather than recurrent capacity alone, drives transfer.
Separates depth information, token information, and their joint trajectory.
Holds the update multiset approximately fixed while removing sequential composition.
Tests interpretable scalar velocity, acceleration, jerk, curvature, and path-length rules before introducing a learned reader.
Uses RealToxicityPrompts-to-ToxiGen transfer to probe robustness beyond the training vocabulary distribution.

evaluations.setting: Llama-3.1-8B; eight source readers over nine reasoning benchmarks
evaluations.metric: Candidate selection accuracy, source ID accuracy, and mean OOD accuracy
evaluations.result: TaT exceeds the exact-middle-layer probe in every donor-row mean; strong donor OOD means are 79.31 (ARC-C), 76.34 (ARC-E), and 76.83 (OpenQA), while BoolQ and SocialIQA donors fall to 53.02 and 64.89
evaluations.baseline: Final-continuation-token linear probe at the exact middle layer; frozen zero-shot average 67.9 and task-specific few-shot average 75.7

evaluations.metric: Transfer selection accuracy on StoryCloze, OpenQA, ARC-E, ARC-C, BoolQ, and HellaSwag
evaluations.result: TaT beats rank-16 LoRA on 5/6 tasks, including 94.98 versus 83.76 on StoryCloze, but loses BoolQ 78.56 versus 79.97
evaluations.baseline: Rank-16 LoRA and the static middle-layer probe

evaluations.setting: RealToxicityPrompts-trained readers on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-14B, Qwen3-30B MoE, and Qwen3-32B
evaluations.metric: ToxiGen OOD accuracy and RealToxicityPrompts standard/challenging accuracy
evaluations.result: Displacement wins ToxiGen for 3/4 models but loses Qwen2.5-14B 82.28 versus 83.48 raw; raw wins all eight in-domain split comparisons
evaluations.baseline: Raw-activation LSTM and static linear probe

evaluations.setting: ARC-C, ARC-E, and OpenQA reasoning donors
evaluations.metric: Average, ID, and OOD selection accuracy
evaluations.result: Raw LSTM beats displacement OOD for ARC-C (83.62 versus 79.31) and narrowly for ARC-E (76.55 versus 76.34); displacement wins OpenQA (76.83 versus 69.85)
evaluations.baseline: Same LSTM on raw trajectories and static linear probe

evaluations.setting: Token-by-layer grid ablations for ARC-C and ARC-E donors
evaluations.result: Full grid is strongest, but ARC-E final-token-only is nearly tied OOD at 76.08 versus 76.34; ARC-C shows a larger 73.68 versus 79.31 gap
evaluations.baseline: Single middle-layer row and final-token column

evaluations.setting: Sequential-order ablation for ARC-C, ARC-E, and OpenQA donors
evaluations.result: LSTM versus Set MLP is 79.31 versus 73.17, 76.34 versus 72.75, and 76.83 versus 72.70
evaluations.baseline: Shared per-update MLP followed by order-invariant mean pooling

evaluations.setting: Qwen2.5-14B appendix grid; OpenQA, ARC-C, and ARC-E donors over four targets
evaluations.metric: ID and mean OOD candidate selection accuracy
evaluations.result: TaT OOD means are 82.65, 83.66, and 85.58 versus probe means 65.97, 74.74, and 72.08
evaluations.baseline: Model-specific static linear probe plus zero- and few-shot frozen-model accuracy

evaluations.metric: Parameters, separate-pass inference time, and memory
evaluations.result: The LSTM adds 4.76M parameters (0.06%), 10.5 ms over a 64.0 ms base pass (16%), and 18.1 MB over about 15 GB (0.12%)
evaluations.baseline: Frozen 8.0B-parameter Llama forward pass; candidate-multiplicity cost is not included

evaluations.setting: Oracle-guided scalar kinematics on four benchmarks for Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-14B
evaluations.metric: Candidate-selection accuracy under ground-truth-selected descriptor rules
evaluations.result: Velocity sometimes beats the frozen model, but no scalar rule transfers consistently; alternative trajectory reductions worsen results
evaluations.baseline: Random selection and frozen normalized-log-likelihood selection

limitations: Author-stated: TaT requires extracting and processing full activation traces across all tokens and layers and is more expensive than a single-layer probe.
Author-stated: the LSTM's learned geometric features remain implicit and lack head- or circuit-level interpretability.
Author-stated: the classifier still needs labeled, generalizable source data; a successful fixed kinematic rule would remove this dependency.

Author-stated: experiments are constrained candidate-selection tasks and do not cover self-generated multi-step reasoning, intermediate error localization, or hallucination detection inside free-form chains.

Reviewer-identified: 'zero-shot' means no target examples in the prompt, not no supervision; each reader is trained on labeled source candidates and cannot be compared directly with an unadapted base-model average as though both used the same information.
Reviewer-identified: the system ranks an enumerated answer set and supplies neither a calibrated standalone correctness score nor abstention, threshold-transfer, or open-ended verification results.

Reviewer-identified: every candidate requires a separate base-model forward pass and full trace, so total latency and memory traffic grow with candidate count; Table 7 measures only the LSTM component in one extraction scheme.

Reviewer-identified: the claimed lexical-confound mechanism is inferred from domain transfer. There are no matched lexical counterfactuals, feature-reconstruction measurements, prompt-template swaps with fixed semantics, or causal interventions.

Reviewer-identified: raw trajectories outperform displacement for two of three reasoning donors and every RealToxicityPrompts ID split, so differencing is a context-dependent regularizer rather than a uniformly superior representation.

Reviewer-identified: the main exact-middle-layer probe is not validation-selected per dataset, even though Appendix D documents meaningful layer sensitivity; this weakens conclusions about all static probes.

Reviewer-identified: the paper reports hyperparameter ranges and three-seed averaging but omits exact learning-rate grids, regularizers, batch sizes, epoch/stopping rules, train/validation counts, and uncertainty bars for the principal accuracy tables.
Reviewer-identified: the supervised UMAP in Figure 1 visually amplifies class separation and cannot independently establish smoother correct trajectories or a task-general invariant.

Reviewer-identified: architecture coverage uses separately trained readers, only a few open base models, and inconsistent Qwen2.5/Qwen3 model names; it does not demonstrate cross-model classifier transfer.

Reviewer-identified: ToxiGen is treated as a proxy for lexical-confound robustness, but the work does not isolate benign quotation, reclaimed language, demographic subgroup errors, calibration, or false-positive costs.
Reviewer-identified: the LoRA comparison is limited to one source task and does not match trainable parameter budget, per-candidate computation, or optimization objective.

Reviewer-identified: current follow-on evidence in arXiv:2608.05660 shows that displacement loses useful state-location information and that adding restricted region and direction streams substantially improves transfer, narrowing the case for displacement alone.
failure_modes: A source dataset with a shallow or idiosyncratic notion of validity can train a reader that transfers poorly, as the BoolQ and SocialIQA donor rows demonstrate.
Persistent content that changes substantially from layer to layer will survive differencing and can remain a lexical or formatting shortcut.
Correctness information encoded primarily in absolute state location or magnitude can be erased by differencing; the raw-trajectory and later state-conditioned results expose this risk.
Flattening token and layer axes can make the recurrent order sensitive to sequence length, tokenizer behavior, padding, or answer-format differences rather than reasoning.
A separate binary score for every candidate may select the right option while all scores are poorly calibrated, preventing standalone verification or safe abstention.
Long prompts, many candidates, and large residual widths can make all-token/all-layer trace storage and repeated forward passes prohibitive.
An unavailable residual stream, model API boundary, quantized deployment, architecture update, or tokenizer change makes the learned reader unusable or requires re-extraction and retraining.
Displacement can underperform raw states on in-domain monitoring, including all reported RealToxicityPrompts ID cells and the large Qwen3-30B-MoE challenging split gap.
The LSTM may exploit a source-specific prompt template or candidate-position pattern even when it outperforms a linear probe on nearby benchmarks.
A model can produce a fluent but invalid free-form chain for which no enumerated countercandidate exists; the reported ranker provides no tested operating procedure in that case.
reusable_insights: Treat adjacent-layer residual updates as a bottlenecked view of computation and always compare them with raw states under the same reader capacity.
Unfold both token and depth axes before deciding that a single token or layer contains the relevant diagnostic signal.
Use a single-donor transfer matrix, not only pooled training, to reveal which sources teach genuinely reusable signals and which sources are brittle.
Pair a sequence-aware reader with an order-invariant set control to test whether composition order matters beyond access to the same updates.
Report full negative screens of interpretable descriptors before replacing them with a learned encoder; the failure pattern constrains later mechanistic claims.
Evaluate a representation bottleneck on both ID and lexical/prompt-shift OOD data because removing absolute state can help transfer while hurting local accuracy.
Separate target-zero-shot transfer from supervision-free inference in terminology and baseline design.
Measure end-to-end cost per complete candidate set, including trace extraction and repeated base passes, rather than only auxiliary-classifier parameters.
open_questions: Can a trajectory reader produce a calibrated, portable correctness probability for one free-form answer without an enumerated candidate set?
Which lexical, token-identity, prompt-format, and answer-length information remains recoverable from displacement embeddings?
Would a state-conditioned motion reader, restricted direction stream, or magnitude channel dominate displacement alone under matched capacity and seeds?
Can causal patching of the token-layer updates that most change the TaT score alter answer correctness, rather than only predict it?
How much of the gain survives a validation-selected best-layer nonlinear static probe and stronger sequence baselines such as small convolutions or attention readers?
Can one shared detector transfer between base models, checkpoints, languages, and tokenizers after an explicit representation alignment?
What is the end-to-end latency and memory traffic for realistic candidate counts, long contexts, and an actually pipelined implementation?
Does TaT detect the first invalid step in model-generated reasoning, adversarially fluent wrong chains, and errors whose final answer happens to be correct?
Which donor properties predict transfer before training, and can donor selection or multi-donor training improve weak-source failures without learning dataset identity?

competitive_landscape.title: Reasoning Errors Have a Region and a Direction in the Residual-Stream Trajectory of LLMs
competitive_landscape.difference: This later paper keeps TaT's displacement reader but shows that motion omits the state from which an update originates. It adds a hard vector-quantized region and normalized multi-depth direction streams, reports up to 12 points over displacement-only transfer, and adds wording-reconstruction, factual-transfer, depth, capacity, and cross-model audits. It therefore confirms the value of trajectory reading while narrowing any claim that displacement alone captures a task-general validity invariant.

competitive_landscape.title: The Geometry of Reasoning: Flowing Logics in Representation Space
competitive_landscape.difference: Zhou et al. already model reasoning as representation-space flows with position, velocity, and curvature and use controlled natural-deduction propositions with semantic carriers to separate logic from surface meaning. TaT changes the operational target to supervised correctness selection over broad benchmark candidates and learns from all token-layer displacements rather than fitting explicit logical flow fields or relying on scalar kinematics.

competitive_landscape.title: The Geometries of Truth Are Orthogonal Across Tasks
competitive_landscape.difference: Azizian et al. show that static correctness probes are task-dependent, nearly orthogonal, and often supported on disjoint activation coordinates; mixtures and multi-task probes do not remove the problem. TaT directly targets this failure with a learned displacement sequence and reports cross-task candidate selection, but does not match their sparsity/subspace analysis or prove that its transferred score is the same feature across tasks.

competitive_landscape.title: Probing the Geometry of Truth: Consistency and Generalization of Truth Directions in LLMs Across Logical Transformations and Question Answering Tasks
competitive_landscape.difference: Bao et al. find that static truth directions can generalize from atomic statements to logical transformations, QA, in-context learning, and external knowledge in sufficiently capable models, and evaluate selective QA. TaT instead reads ordered updates for multi-candidate reasoning and toxicity; it offers broader donor-target grids but no selective-risk, calibration, or direct comparison with their stronger truth-probe recipes.

competitive_landscape.title: Reasoning Models Know When They're Right: Probing Hidden States for Self-Verification
competitive_landscape.difference: Zhang et al. probe reasoning-model hidden states for current and future intermediate-answer correctness, report calibrated scores, and use them for early exit with 24% fewer tokens. TaT focuses on frozen base-model candidate ranking and cross-benchmark transfer using the whole layer trajectory; it neither verifies online intermediate steps nor demonstrates calibrated early stopping.

competitive_landscape.title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets
competitive_landscape.difference: Marks and Tegmark establish transferable linear truth structure on true/false statements and add causal activation interventions, with simple difference-in-means probes competitive with more complex probes. TaT replaces one static vector with a nonlinear reader over depthwise motion and evaluates reasoning options and toxicity, but supplies correlation and selection evidence rather than causal control.

competitive_landscape.title: Curved Inference: Concern-Sensitive Geometry in Large Language Model Residual Streams
competitive_landscape.difference: Manson measures native-space curvature and salience under an unembedding-derived pullback metric on 20 matched concern-shift prompts and two small models. TaT scales from descriptive geometric statistics to a supervised LSTM correctness/toxicity reader on standard datasets, but it discards metric interpretability and does not isolate semantic concern with matched prompts.

competitive_landscape.title: Transformer Dynamics: A neuroscientific approach to interpretability of large language models
competitive_landscape.difference: Fernando and Guitchounts conceptualize the residual stream as a dynamical system across layers and document continuity, acceleration, density, curved low-dimensional paths, and attractor-like lower-layer behavior. TaT borrows this depth-as-time view but contributes a task-supervised displacement sequence classifier and cross-dataset validity experiments rather than a descriptive dynamical-systems characterization.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim the first approach to unfold every token's activations across every layer into a continuous trajectory for reasoning-validity detection, with layerwise displacement exposing task-agnostic geometric invariants that outperform static probes and extend to toxicity.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Prior work already establishes residual streams as depthwise dynamical systems, geometric reasoning flows, curvature/velocity descriptors, linear truth directions, cross-task failures of static probes, and hidden-state self-verification. The paper's empirical addition is the specific N-by-L displacement construction, lightweight learned sequence reader, single-donor transfer grids, and matched raw/grid/order controls. Its own tables show that raw trajectories can beat displacement, weak donors fail, the few-shot comparison is not consistently won, and ToxiGen displacement is not uniformly best.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty is a practical supervised all-token/all-layer displacement reader for candidate-level transfer, plus an unusually broad set of initial reasoning, toxicity, grid, order, and architecture tests. It does not establish a universal, causal, calibration-ready geometry of truth; 'task-agnostic invariant' should be narrowed to an empirically transferable ranking signal under particular donors and frozen models. By 2026-08-23, the direct follow-on arXiv:2608.05660 further narrows displacement-only novelty by showing that restricted state region and direction recover substantial signal that TaT discards.
